strengths: Addresses a timely problem: sparse expert specialization for heterogeneous federated clients, including unseen clients without labeled test-time fine-tuning.
The high-level design—frozen shared encoder, learned router, sparse top-K expert dispatch, and anchor-based warm-up—is intuitive and potentially useful.

Experiments span four datasets, vision and text, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental-client settings, and several ablations. DDOME reports substantial gains in some configurations and includes a useful equal-expert-count comparison with FedMix.
The paper is generally readable, and it candidly identifies dependence on the common expert, anchor selection, communication overhead, scalability, and fairness as limitations.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not established. It only considers one experts-then-router procedure and never proves joint training succeeds. More seriously, the proof evaluates the initial routing indicators rather than the optimized router from Eq. (2), reverses an inequality on page 25, drops the routing-overlap probability in the final loss bound, and uses inconsistent Gaussian scalings and conditions on m. The stated theorem is even false for the permitted case m=1.

The strongest experiments depend on anchor clients deliberately constructed from disjoint label groups and assigned one-to-one to experts; their expert-ID loss effectively supplies coarse task supervision. Performance without anchors is poor. This substantially weakens the claim that specialization is discovered from implicit heterogeneity without task partitions.

The comparison is insufficiently controlled. Main tables compare a 5–10-model personalized system against mostly single global models, omit many modern personalized or clustered FL baselines, and report no repeated-run uncertainty. Several baselines catastrophically degrade from the pretrained checkpoint; the authors acknowledge a learning-rate mismatch, while DDOME alone receives a different optimizer and decay schedule for text.

The reported 'gating accuracy' is just final classification correctness, not routing quality relative to the best available expert. There is no direct joint-versus-disjoint training ablation or convincing quantitative analysis of expert diversity and specialization.

Communication and efficiency claims are qualitative: bytes, FLOPs, latency, memory, common-encoder computation, and test-time transfer of K full experts are not measured. DDOME is explicitly more expensive than single-model FL and requires over 100 hours for the text experiment.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of code and important details such as exact pretrained checkpoints, encoder feature layer, router dimensions, learning-rate decay, baseline tuning ranges, aggregation weights, seeds, and checkpoint-selection protocol. The privacy-preserving characterization is also unsupported by a threat model or protection against model-update leakage.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant problem: dynamically specializing and sparsely communicating experts in heterogeneous decentralized learning.
DDOME combines a frozen common encoder, learned routing, sparse expert transmission, and an anchor-based warm start in a concrete end-to-end algorithm.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering CIFAR-10/100, EMNIST, and Yahoo! Answers, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental-learning scenarios, and sensitivity analyses for common-expert quality and anchor frequency.
The reported accuracy gains are large, and the paper usefully acknowledges dependence on pretrained representations, communication overhead, initialization, and tuning.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is not reliable. Theorem 1 includes m=1, for which expert-first training trivially recovers the sole ground-truth expert and contradicts the claimed constant error. The proof also analyzes the initialized routing regions rather than the router optimized in the theorem's second stage, defines the learned and ground-truth indicators identically, mixes high-probability statements with expectations over the same initialization, uses stronger dimension restrictions than the theorem states, and contains unsupported or reversed inequalities. It therefore does not establish that joint training is necessary.

The claimed emergence of specialization without explicit task partitions is undermined by the essential anchor mechanism. Anchors are deliberately constructed to have distinct or disjoint label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, heavily oversampled, and used to provide one-hot supervision to the gate. Performance largely fails without anchors, so the main evidence demonstrates specialization from privileged label-structured supervision rather than discovery from implicit heterogeneity.

The evaluation is not sufficiently reliable: there are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests despite highly variable curves. Checkpoint selection alternates among final accuracy, best accuracy, and the best of the last ten rounds. Several baselines catastrophically degrade from strong pretrained checkpoints, and the authors explicitly attribute this partly to mismatched learning rates; DDOME alone receives a special decay schedule. These results do not support state-of-the-art claims.

Comparisons are capacity- and methodologically mismatched. DDOME maintains 5–10 experts while the main FedMix comparison uses only two, and strong personalized, clustered, and contemporary federated-MoE baselines are largely absent. A single K-means visualization is insufficient to dismiss clustering approaches.

Communication and efficiency claims are not quantified in bytes, FLOPs, latency, memory, or total training cost. The analysis omits transmitting and running the common encoder and gate, processing or storing every client's embeddings, and maintaining a larger server-side expert pool. Relative to single-model FL, each selected client communicates multiple full experts.

The purported zero-shot setting is narrow and partly transductive: test clients contain new combinations of already-seen classes, and routing uses the entire client's unlabeled test set. This does not substantiate broader claims about unseen domains or tasks.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code link, and important details are missing, including exact pretrained checkpoints, gate width, decay schedule, seeds, split generation, per-client sample counts, aggregation weighting for sparsely updated experts, hyperparameter-search protocols, and consistent checkpoint-selection rules. The pseudocode and presentation also contain undefined or mislabeled items such as FedJETs, duplicated citations, and ambiguous duplicate accuracy columns.

The paper calls FL privacy-preserving without a threat model or privacy mechanism. Routing decisions and updates may reveal client-distribution information, while fairness and specialization-induced bias receive only a brief qualitative discussion.

strengths: The manuscript tackles a relevant problem: adaptive expert routing for heterogeneous, previously unseen federated clients. The top-K transfer mechanism could provide useful personalization and communication tradeoffs if validated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-w5kcnqwh/call-a583dfbab3564f79acc3ccbaf0118ec6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
DDOME combines a frozen common encoder, a lightweight learned ranker, sparse expert dispatch, and joint local updates in a coherent and generally understandable framework.
The empirical study spans four image/text datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental-client scenarios, and several ablations. The reported accuracy gains are substantial.

The paper reports basic optimization, hardware, and runtime details and candidly acknowledges dependence on the common expert, scalability and tuning limitations, additional communication versus single-model FL, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is invalid as written. Theorem 1 permits m=1, for which expert-first training exactly recovers the sole ground-truth expert, directly contradicting both conclusions. The statement also mixes a high-probability claim over router initialization with an expectation over that same randomness. In the proof, the input covariance changes from I/sqrt(d) to I/d; an unproved assumption absent from the theorem is introduced; a maximum is incorrectly replaced by an infinity norm; the key inequality on page 25 is reversed; and the final loss bound drops probability and covariance factors. Thus the paper does not establish that joint training is necessary.

The claimed discovery of specialization from implicit heterogeneity without task boundaries conflicts with the main experimental construction. Anchor clients are deliberately assigned non-overlapping label groups covering the classes, mapped one-to-one to experts, and used to train the gate with explicit one-hot expert identities. This injects precisely the task/expert supervision the motivating claim says is unavailable.

There is little direct evidence that semantic specialization occurs. Per-expert global accuracies do not show that experts learn distinct functions, and Table 5 reports prediction correctness rather than routing correctness. Missing evaluations include routing entropy or expert-domain alignment, random/frozen versus learned gates, joint versus sequential training, and a simple supervised label-partition or oracle-routing baseline.

Experimental uncertainty is not assessed: the paper gives no independent-run statistics, error bars, or significance tests despite stochastic client construction and optimization. Reporting also mixes averages, the best test accuracy during training, and the best of the final ten test evaluations; selecting checkpoints by test accuracy risks optimistic test-set tuning.

The comparisons do not establish state of the art. Main-table FedMix uses only two total experts while DDOME uses five or ten, despite both transmitting two experts per client. Several baselines collapse far below their pretrained starting checkpoint, raising substantial tuning and checkpointing concerns. Relevant personalized or mixture/clustered FL methods are largely absent, and the matched-expert experiment covers only one CIFAR-10 setting without repeated trials.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a method whose results strongly depend on initialization. The manuscript does not specify how the task-specific common checkpoints were trained or what data they used, exact gate architecture, complete sample allocations, aggregation weighting, seeds, or checkpoint-selection rules, and provides no code. The stated sampling “with replacement” also leaves possible train-client duplication unclear.

The communication claim is not empirically quantified in bytes, cumulative traffic, computation, memory, or latency. In the main comparison DDOME and FedMix each transmit two full experts per selected client, while DDOME additionally communicates a gate, so reduced communication is not demonstrated under the reported matched transfer count.

At test time, expert selection aggregates embeddings from the new client's entire local test collection. This is a transductive client-level adaptation signal rather than conventional per-example zero-shot inference and should be identified and compared against baselines receiving analogous information. Separately, describing the setup as privacy-preserving is unsupported without a threat model, privacy analysis, secure aggregation, or differential privacy.

The evaluation spans image and text classification, multiple synthetic heterogeneity schemes, unseen clients, incremental-learning scenarios, and ablations of the common expert and anchor-client ratio. Results within these constructed settings are sometimes substantial.
The authors disclose useful limitations, hardware and approximate training time, dependence on common-expert quality, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central premise is not convincingly demonstrated. Main experiments construct anchors using label knowledge—often partitioning labels without replacement—and explicitly train the router toward one-hot anchor–expert assignments. Specialization is therefore strongly supervised by engineered task structure, contrary to claims that it emerges from implicit heterogeneity without task definitions.

Theorem 1 is not established. As stated, m=1 is an immediate counterexample; it also combines probability and expectation over the same initialization incoherently and omits an assumption used by the proof. The appendix contains reversed or unsupported inequalities, incorrect indices, unresolved equation references, and drops probability factors in the final loss bound. Its auxiliary covariance assumption is unproved and false in its stated generality.

Even a repaired theorem would only show failure of one expert-first-then-router procedure for a population linear-Gaussian top-1 model. It neither proves that joint training succeeds nor analyzes DDOME's pretrained encoder, top-K routing, anchor supervision, aggregation, or convergence. No direct joint-versus-sequential experimental ablation bridges this gap.

The claimed state-of-the-art gains are not supported by a credible comparison. Several baselines collapse far below the unchanged common expert; the authors acknowledge an inconsistent learning rate for FedAvg, fail to obtain a usable SCAFFOLD model, and give DDOME a different optimizer schedule for text. Recent personalized, clustered, and federated-MoE methods are largely omitted. In some appendix comparisons, DDOME itself underperforms the no-training common expert.

There are no results across random seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Reporting alternates among averages, best accuracy during training, and best values from the last ten test evaluations, raising test-set model-selection concerns. Specialization is not directly measured: Table 5 appears to report downstream classification correctness rather than router accuracy against a defined oracle, and random, oracle, or simple common-expert class-routing baselines are absent.

The communication-efficiency claim is qualitative only. No transmitted-byte, memory, latency, or accuracy-versus-communication analysis is provided. In the main comparison, both FedMix and DDOME transmit two experts per client, while DDOME benefits from a larger server-side pool and additionally communicates a router; it also costs more than single-model methods.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code, seeds, exact common-expert checkpoints or pretraining procedure, router hidden size/activation, precise client sample counts, checkpoint-selection rule, aggregation weighting, or baseline-tuning protocol. Sampling data with replacement further makes the effective datasets and weighting ambiguous.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem: sparse, personalized expert selection in decentralized learning, with the practical goal of reducing per-client model transmission. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2bgwafno/call-1200372af49a42ae8aa4a357dbeea41a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
DDOME is a concrete system combining a frozen common encoder, a learned router, a pool of experts, top-K dispatch, and anchor-client bootstrapping. The overall workflow is reasonably intuitive.

The experiments cover vision and text datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, changing client pools, routing accuracy, and ablations of common-expert quality and anchor frequency. Several reported improvements are substantial.
The authors explicitly acknowledge dependence on a strong pretrained model, additional communication relative to single-model FL, limited scale, tuning complexity, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central claim of discovering specialization from implicit heterogeneity without explicit task boundaries is contradicted by the main setup. Anchor clients are deliberately constructed around distinct label groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, given one-hot expert-ID supervision, and heavily oversampled. Thus, the method explicitly seeds class-based specialization rather than demonstrating that it emerges.

Theorem 1 is false or at least seriously incomplete as stated. The allowed m=1 case makes routing trivial and expert-first training exactly recovers the sole ground-truth expert, contradicting both lower bounds. The input covariance changes from 1/sqrt(d) in Section 3 to 1/d in the proof, also invalidating the assertion that labels and loss have constant scale.

The appendix proof contains additional material gaps: its key covariance assumption is unproved, omitted from the theorem, and implausible for arbitrary positive-definite covariance; Lemma 1 is applied to a subspace containing V* without an assumption relating W* and V*; a derived inequality gives ||zeta|| <= ||hat-zeta|| but is subsequently used in the opposite direction; indices, probability statements, and dimensional conditions are inconsistent; and two referenced equations remain marked '(??)'.

Even a repaired theorem would only show failure of one specific experts-first, router-second procedure. It neither establishes that every decoupled strategy fails nor proves that joint training succeeds, so it cannot justify the claimed necessity of joint training. Correspondingly, the experiments lack a controlled joint-versus-decoupled DDOME ablation.

The baseline comparison is not adequately controlled. DDOME maintains 5–10 experts while major baselines use one model and FedMix usually uses two; parameter count, FLOPs, memory, and transmitted bytes are not matched or reported. In the main tables both DDOME and FedMix transmit two experts per client, so the advertised communication reduction is not demonstrated empirically. DDOME also receives a different optimizer and learning-rate decay in the text experiment.

The baseline results raise substantial reliability concerns: several methods catastrophically degrade strong pretrained checkpoints, tuning details are vague, and modern personalized, clustered, and federated-MoE alternatives are largely absent. In one domain-generalization comparison, the untouched common expert substantially outperforms DDOME and every cited method.

Results provide no independent-run statistics, error bars, or significance tests despite stochastic partitioning and visibly unstable trajectories. Some appendix tables report the 'best' accuracy or best values over late rounds, creating checkpoint-selection ambiguity.

The evaluation uses synthetic class-skew partitions and aggregates an entire unseen client's unlabeled test set—up to thousands of samples—to choose experts. This is transductive routing rather than convincingly demonstrated just-in-time personalization, and the number and construction of test clients are insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code or checkpoint link, and important details such as common-expert provenance and training, exact gate dimensions, decay schedule, baseline hyperparameters, seeds, partition files, aggregation weighting, and model-selection protocol are missing.

Presentation errors further reduce confidence: multiple plots label the proposed method 'FedJETs' rather than DDOME, table columns are ambiguously duplicated as 'Acc.', several references are duplicated or mismatched, and the pseudocode contains malformed gradients and underspecified aggregation. Privacy is asserted as a benefit without threat-model or leakage analysis.

The empirical comparison is not sufficient for a state-of-the-art claim. Important personalized and clustered FL methods are omitted; clustering is dismissed using only one qualitative K-means plot. FedMix generally receives fewer total experts than DDOME, optimizer schedules differ across methods, and baseline tuning and checkpoint-selection protocols are inadequately documented.

The communication claim is not demonstrated with transmitted bytes, total communication, latency, or computation. In the main comparison both FedMix and DDOME transmit two experts per selected client, while DDOME additionally communicates a router, requires a common encoder, and stores a larger server-side pool.

Results lack repeated seeds, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests, despite stochastic partitions and sometimes small margins. Reporting alternates among final, best, and average accuracy. Essential reproducibility details are missing, including exact common-expert checkpoints, gate dimensions, test-client construction and sizes, aggregation weighting, top-K gradient handling, and code. Unresolved references such as '(??)' and figures still labeled 'FedJETs' further indicate incompleteness.

Moreover, federated training alone does not establish the paper's privacy-preserving claim, and routing signals may expose client-distribution information.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: communication-efficient personalization in decentralized MoEs. Its combination of a frozen common encoder, client-level routing, sparse expert transfer, and anchor clients is intuitive and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers four vision and text datasets, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, unseen clients, and incremental-client settings. Ablations on common-expert quality, anchor ratio, and matched numbers of experts reveal useful behaviors and failure modes.

Some reported accuracy gains are large under the chosen setup. The paper also provides pseudocode, core optimization settings, hardware/runtime information, and an explicit discussion of limitations and fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is invalid as written. The input scaling is inconsistent between Section 3 and the appendix, and either stated scaling contradicts the claimed constant lower bound: with unit-norm experts, a zero predictor has vanishing MSE as dimension grows. The proof additionally drops covariance and routing-probability factors in its final bound, contains reversed inequalities and index inconsistencies, relies on assumptions absent from the theorem, changes the condition on m, and does not properly analyze the reoptimized second-stage router. Consequently, the claimed necessity of joint training is not established.

The experiments undermine the headline claim of specialization from implicit heterogeneity without task boundaries. All benchmarks use synthetic label skew; anchors are deliberately constructed with distinct or nonoverlapping label groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, and used to supervise the gate with expert IDs. No practical anchor-selection algorithm is given, and performance frequently fails without anchors. Thus explicit prior structure is central to the observed specialization.

Comparisons are not adequately capacity- or optimization-matched. The main tables give DDOME 5 or 10 total experts but FedMix only 2, although both transmit K=2 experts. FedAvg is allowed to deteriorate from a 93% common checkpoint to 58.4%, with the authors acknowledging a learning-rate mismatch, while DDOME receives an algorithm-specific schedule. The matched M=K appendix often remains below the initial common expert. Moreover, specialized personalized, clustered, and recent federated-MoE baselines are largely absent, so the state-of-the-art claim is unsupported.

There are no independent repetitions, error bars, or statistical tests. Several appendix results select the best test accuracy during training, amounting to test-set model selection. The provenance and training data of the strong common experts are unclear, as are important gate dimensions, decay settings, split seeds, aggregation details, and baseline searches; no code is provided.

The unseen-client protocol is transductive and asymmetric: DDOME aggregates router scores over all local test inputs before making predictions, giving it unlabeled batch-level information about the test-client distribution that the global baselines do not receive. Comparable unlabeled adaptation or routing baselines are missing.

Communication and systems-efficiency claims are not empirically substantiated. The paper reports no transmitted bytes, model sizes, client memory, latency, or compute accounting for the common expert, gate, K full experts, and cached embeddings.

The paper does not directly test its main causal claim through joint-versus-sequential, frozen-router, or random-router ablations, nor does it provide a well-defined metric of routing correctness or expert specialization. Thin prior-work coverage, unresolved equation references, notation errors, and figures that still label the method as “FedJETs” further reduce clarity.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a timely problem: adaptive expert specialization and sparse routing for heterogeneous federated clients.
DDOME combines a fixed encoder, client-level top-K expert dispatch, joint local optimization, and anchor-based bootstrapping in an intuitive framework.
The experiments span four image/text datasets, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, and several ablations, with large reported gains over the evaluated baselines.
The paper provides basic optimization and hardware details and candidly acknowledges dependence on a strong common expert, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not supported by a valid proof. Under the stated Gaussian covariance, the label variance—and hence even the trivial loss—vanishes with dimension, contradicting the claimed dimension-independent lower bound. The main text and appendix also use inconsistent covariance scalings. Further problems include an unstated and unproved assumption, probability and expectation over the same initialization, incorrect inequality directions, a changed condition on m, dropping the routing-region probability in the final loss bound, and analyzing the initial router rather than the optimized router from Equation 2. Failure of one experts-then-router procedure also does not establish that joint training is generally necessary, especially without a positive result for joint training.

The claim that specialization arises from implicit heterogeneity without task definitions is overstated. In the principal quantity-based setup, anchor clients are deliberately constructed with distinct non-overlapping label subsets, assigned one-to-one expert targets, and trained with one-hot expert supervision. Anchors constitute 30–50% of every round despite being a small fraction of clients, and the method often fails without them. This is substantial prior structure and oversampling, with no adequate matched control.

The empirical results lack statistical support: there are no run counts, seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several tables select the best test accuracy during training or within the final evaluation rounds, apparently using the test set for checkpoint selection. “Average” is insufficiently defined, and partitioning samples with replacement further obscures effective sample sizes.

Resource comparisons are not controlled. DDOME maintains multiple full ResNet-34 or TinyBERT experts plus a common encoder and gate, while several baselines use one model. The paper reports no parameter-normalized accuracy, communicated bytes, FLOPs, memory, latency, or end-to-end cost, so the communication and efficiency claims are unsubstantiated.

The provenance and training data of the high-accuracy common checkpoints are unspecified, despite their being critical to routing and performance. Baseline tuning is also inadequately documented; DDOME receives a different optimizer schedule for text, while failures such as SCAFFOLD collapse are reported without sufficient settings or diagnosis.

The paper does not directly establish expert specialization or routing quality. It lacks expert-usage, routing-confusion, diversity, oracle-routing, random-routing, frozen-router, and joint-versus-disjoint ablations. Table 5 reports final prediction errors rather than whether the gate selected an appropriate expert.

Reproducibility and positioning are weak: no code artifact is provided, and important details such as gate dimensions, preprocessing, checkpoint construction, partial-expert aggregation, client sample counts, and baseline searches are missing. Coverage of personalized, clustered, multitask, and recent federated-MoE work is limited, weakening the originality and state-of-the-art claims. There are also notable presentation errors, including figures labeling DDOME as “FedJETs” and an AlexNet citation for Average Ensembles.

No severe ethical issue is apparent, and bias is acknowledged, but describing the approach as privacy-preserving is unsupported: ordinary federated parameter exchange provides no formal privacy without a threat model, differential privacy, or secure aggregation, and repeatedly sampling anchor clients may increase their exposure.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem: adaptive expert specialization and communication-efficient routing under decentralized data heterogeneity.

The combination of a frozen common encoder, learned sparse routing, and anchor clients is intuitive and potentially useful. Selecting K<M experts could reduce communication relative to transmitting an entire expert pool.
The evaluation spans image and text classification, multiple heterogeneity constructions, unseen-client evaluation, incremental settings, and ablations of common-expert quality and anchor frequency.
The high-level system and algorithm are presented clearly, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on a strong pretrained expert, communication overhead, and limited scale.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not established by its proof. Among other issues, the appendix defines the learned and ground-truth routing indicators identically, changes the theorem's dimensional condition, uses unsupported concentration probabilities, reverses a key inequality on the auxiliary vector, omits covariance-scaling and region-probability factors in the loss bound, and applies a projection bound that need not hold when expert and router ground-truth vectors align. Most importantly, it never analyzes the router obtained in the theorem's second optimization stage. Consequently, neither the claimed Ω(1) sequential-training loss nor the broader necessity of joint training follows. The paper also provides no positive theorem showing that joint training succeeds.

The claimed emergence of specialization from implicit heterogeneity is undermined by strong explicit supervision: anchor clients are selected for distinct or non-overlapping label distributions, permanently assigned one-to-one to experts, and train the router using one-hot expert identities. They comprise 30–50% of every round, and the method largely fails without them. This is much closer to injecting known task structure than discovering latent specialization without task boundaries.

The experimental comparisons are not controlled adequately. DDOME uses 5–10 stored experts while FedMix uses two and most baselines use one; parameter count, training compute, inference compute, and total communication are not matched. DDOME also receives a different optimizer and learning-rate schedule on Yahoo. Catastrophic degradation of strong pretrained baselines suggests inadequate tuning or checkpoint selection, and several relevant personalized, clustered, and federated-mixture methods are absent.

There are no repeated-run statistics, error bars, confidence intervals, or seed information. Results variously use averages, final checkpoints, the best accuracy during training, or the last ten evaluations, without a validation-based selection protocol. The two accuracy columns in the main tables are poorly labeled, client sample sizes are unclear, and CIFAR10's five test clients each contain 4,000 examples despite a 10,000-example test set, indicating unexplained reuse. Training samples are also assigned to clients with replacement.

The paper does not directly ablate its main thesis: there is no joint-versus-sequential/frozen-router comparison, nor adequate random, fixed, or oracle-routing controls. It reports classification accuracy rather than routing correctness, expert utilization, diversity, specialization, or oracle-routing gap, so the asserted mechanism is not demonstrated.

Efficiency claims are unsupported by measurements of transmitted bytes, FLOPs, latency, memory, or energy. In the reported main configuration, DDOME downloads two experts plus a router, while FedMix also transmits two experts and a single-model baseline transmits one. At inference it must run the full common model for routing and another full expert for prediction, so reduced inference cost is not demonstrated.

Generality is limited to 100-client simulations with synthetically constructed label skew and classification tasks. The unseen-client procedure uses the client's entire unlabeled test batch to select experts, making it transductive rather than ordinary per-example zero-shot evaluation. Natural client heterogeneity, feature shifts, larger deployments, and large-scale MoEs are not tested.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code is provided, and pretrained checkpoint identities, preprocessing details, run counts, learning-rate decay, FedProx coefficient, aggregation weighting, exact anchor-selection procedure, and checkpoint-selection protocol are missing. Citation quality also needs correction: several references are duplicated, the citation used for Average Ensembles points to AlexNet, and FedJETs appears in figures without definition or citation.

The discussion acknowledges fairness risks, but the description of the approach as privacy-preserving lacks a threat model or privacy mechanism; routing choices and model updates may reveal client-distribution information. This is not an unresolved severe ethical issue, but the privacy claim should be substantially qualified.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: communication-aware personalization and expert routing under heterogeneous federated data.

DDOME is an intuitively coherent combination of a frozen encoder, client-conditioned routing, sparse expert transfer, and anchor-based bootstrapping. The high-level workflow is reasonably easy to follow.
The evaluation spans vision and text datasets, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, and several useful ablations. The reported accuracy gains are large if the evaluation is taken at face value.
The authors candidly acknowledge dependence on a strong common expert, additional communication, limited scalability testing, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is unsound as written. Theorem 1 already fails for the allowed case m=1, where the sole expert recovers the sole ground-truth linear predictor. The proof also changes the input covariance from 1/sqrt(d) to 1/d, drops corresponding covariance and routing-probability factors in the final loss bound, uses unjustified or reversed inequalities, and invokes an unproved assumption omitted from the theorem statement.

Even a corrected theorem would only show failure of one specific experts-first-then-router procedure. It neither establishes that joint training is necessary among all decoupled or alternating procedures nor proves that joint training or DDOME successfully recovers specialization. Its setting is also far removed from DDOME's soft, client-level routing, anchors, nonlinear experts, and federated optimization.

The empirical premise of discovering specialization without explicit task boundaries is contradicted by the anchor mechanism. Main experiments deliberately construct anchors from distinct label groups, assign them one-to-one to experts, and train the gate using one-hot expert identities. Performance deteriorates sharply without this explicit routing supervision.

The paper does not directly demonstrate its core specialization claim. It lacks joint-versus-disjoint training ablations and convincing measurements of routing quality, load balance, expert diversity, or semantic allocation. Table 5 reports final classification errors rather than correctness of expert selection.

Comparisons do not support the state-of-the-art claim. Main results give DDOME 5-10 experts while FedMix receives 2 and other baselines receive one model; relevant personalized, clustered, and federated-MoE methods are largely absent. Several baselines catastrophically forget strong pretrained checkpoints, and the paper itself attributes this partly to inconsistent learning rates, suggesting inadequate tuning.

The communication-efficiency claim is not measured. In the main comparison, both DDOME and FedMix transmit two experts per client, while DDOME additionally requires a common encoder, a gate, and an extra routing exchange. There are no byte, FLOP, memory, latency, or accuracy-versus-communication results.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are inadequate: there are no run counts, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests; some tables select the best test accuracy during training without a validation protocol; and code, seeds, common-expert training details, gate dimensions, decay schedule, and exact partition/checkpoint procedures are missing. Multiple plots label the proposed curve as the otherwise undefined "FedJETs," further obscuring interpretation.

Evidence is limited to synthetic label-skew partitions of standard classification datasets with 100 clients. The method requires identifying distinctive, repeatedly available anchor clients and processing an unseen client's full unlabeled local set, so broader claims about realistic decentralized deployment and just-in-time personalization are premature. Federated learning is also described as privacy-preserving without a threat model or privacy mechanism.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: dynamically routing a small subset of experts for heterogeneous, previously unseen federated clients without test-time labels.
DDOME combines a frozen feature encoder, learned routing, sparse expert communication, and anchor clients in a conceptually coherent system with useful pseudocode.
The empirical scope is broad, covering CIFAR-10/100, EMNIST, Yahoo! Answers, two non-IID partition schemes, incremental settings, and ablations of anchors and common-expert quality.

Reported accuracy improvements are substantial in several settings, and the paper candidly acknowledges dependence on the common expert, communication overhead, and limited scalability. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-wik8bllk/call-be89f601a1f041f195e2db5f5aaae7ca/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central theorem is not technically supported. It only studies one sequential procedure and never proves that joint training succeeds or is necessary. Moreover, the statement is false for the permitted case m=1, where the sole expert recovers the ground-truth linear predictor exactly.

The proof contains fatal inconsistencies: the learned and ground-truth routing indicators are defined identically; the optimized second-stage router is not analyzed; probability and expectation are conflated; the proof requires a stricter m/d regime than the theorem states; an inequality bounding ζ is reversed and then used in the opposite direction; and the final loss bound drops the routing-region intersection probability. Additional unmentioned assumptions on the relationship between the two orthonormal parameter sets are also used.

The claimed emergence of specialization without explicit task information is undermined by the anchor construction. Anchors are deliberately selected to cover distinct label groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, and train the gate with expert-ID one-hot targets. The no-anchor ablation performs poorly, indicating that this privileged label-based supervision is central rather than incidental.

The evaluation is not statistically reliable: there are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Several appendices report the best test accuracy during training or test-accuracy envelopes without a validation-based selection protocol, creating potential test-set selection bias.

Baseline comparisons are insufficient and potentially unfair. DDOME has 5–10 total experts versus one model for several baselines and two for FedMix; many relevant personalized, clustered, and federated-MoE methods are absent. The paper acknowledges inconsistent learning rates for pretrained baselines, gives DDOME a different optimizer schedule on Yahoo!, and reports unexplained catastrophic failures for several baselines without adequate tuning details.

The task-specific common experts have high CIFAR, EMNIST, and Yahoo! accuracies, but their training data, checkpoint construction, and possible overlap with federated data are unspecified. This prevents reproduction and could invalidate the decentralized premise if centralized task data were used. The observed performance threshold also contradicts claims of being agnostic to common-expert performance.

Communication and efficiency claims are qualitative. No bytes, parameter counts, FLOPs, latency, client memory, or total communication-to-target-accuracy are reported; DDOME transmits two experts plus a gate and requires the frozen common expert, so it may be more expensive than single-model baselines.

Specialization itself is not convincingly measured: there are no expert utilization, diversity, class-conditional competence, collapse, or routing-oracle analyses, and the definition of a “correct” expert in the per-sample routing table is unclear. A direct joint-versus-disjoint training ablation is also missing.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite some hyperparameter and hardware details: no code is provided, and gate dimensions, common-expert provenance, exact aggregation, seeds, partition files, checkpoint selection, and sample-with-replacement behavior remain unclear. Figures also refer to the method as “FedJETs,” and several citations are duplicated or incorrect.

The claim that the setup is privacy-preserving is not substantiated by differential privacy, secure aggregation, or leakage analysis. Expert-selection identities and gate/model updates may reveal client distributions, while the fairness discussion does not address the disproportionate participation burden and influence of anchor clients.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: communication-efficient, adaptive expert specialization under decentralized data heterogeneity.
DDOME is a concrete end-to-end design combining a frozen feature extractor, learned routing, sparse expert transmission, anchor-based stabilization, and label-free inference for unseen clients.
The empirical study spans four image/text datasets, two non-IID partition schemes, incremental-client scenarios, and several ablations. Some reported accuracy gains are substantial.
The paper reports hardware and training time, acknowledges dependence on the common expert and anchors, and discusses possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. Theorem 1 addresses only one particular expert-first training procedure, provides no result showing joint training succeeds, and therefore cannot justify a general “necessity” claim. More seriously, the appendix appears not to analyze the optimized router from Eq. (2), instead reusing indicators associated with the initial router.

The proof contains material inconsistencies and invalid steps: the Gaussian covariance scaling conflicts between the theorem and appendix and contradicts the claim that labels have constant magnitude; the stated condition m <= sqrt(d) is used as m <= sqrt(d)/2; probability and expectation over the initialization are conflated; covariance factors are omitted; and the final loss lower bound drops routing-overlap probabilities and uses problematic projection inequalities. Even m=1 contradicts the stated constant-error conclusion.

The claimed absence of task definitions is undermined by the anchor construction. Anchors are deliberately selected to have distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, and oversampled. This injects explicit label-structure supervision and may itself explain specialization and much of the gain.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed mechanism. There is no decisive comparison of joint training against sequential training, a fixed or random router, frozen components, or an anchor-matched non-MoE control. Table 5 reports classification errors rather than a clearly defined routing-accuracy target, and no convincing expert-specialization or routing-load analysis is provided.

Baseline and efficiency comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Main comparisons use 5–10 DDOME experts versus two FedMix experts, text baselines receive different optimization schedules, anchor sampling changes data exposure, and relevant personalized/clustered federated-learning baselines are largely absent. Communication is asserted rather than measured in bytes, total rounds, computation, latency, or end-to-end cost, including the common encoder and router.

The empirical evidence lacks repeated-seed means, uncertainty estimates, and significance testing. Several results report the best test accuracy or repeatedly inspect test accuracy during training, creating possible test-set model-selection bias. Important reproduction details—checkpoint provenance, pretraining data, decay schedule, MLP dimensions, baseline tuning, random seeds, and code—are missing.

External validity is limited to synthetic label-skew partitions with 100 clients and classification tasks. Performance depends strongly on a high-quality common model with target-dataset accuracy, while its acquisition and realistic federated availability are insufficiently explained.

The presentation contains notable reliability issues, including inconsistent method naming in figures, duplicated or questionable citations, unresolved equation references, and numerous notation errors. The privacy-preserving characterization is also too strong without secure aggregation, differential privacy, or analysis of update leakage.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: personalized, communication-aware MoE training under decentralized non-IID data. Its combination of a frozen common encoder, client-conditioned routing, sparse expert dispatch, and anchor clients is intuitive and practically motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-zy936xbp/call-521a62dea6c743e5a4c2933fddd52e15/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical study spans CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, EMNIST, and Yahoo! Answers, with quantity-based and Dirichlet label skew, incremental-client scenarios, and several ablations. The reported gains are substantial within the authors' setup.
The common-expert-quality and anchor-client-ratio studies expose meaningful failure modes, including a routing phase transition and collapse without sufficient anchoring.

The paper reports major optimization settings, hardware and approximate training times, and candidly acknowledges dependence on a strong pretrained encoder, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness harms.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is false as stated. It permits m=1, in which case the sole routing region is the entire input space, population least squares recovers the sole ground-truth expert exactly, and the loss is zero—contradicting both claimed constant lower bounds.

Even beyond that counterexample, the proof is not valid. It contains unresolved equation references, an incorrect concentration-tail statement, silently strengthens m≤√d to stricter conditions, and defines the learned and ground-truth routing indicators identically. More seriously, it bounds a subspace containing the ground-truth router as though it were random relative to the ground-truth experts, reverses the inequality needed in the ζ argument, analyzes the initialized routing cells rather than the optimized second-stage router, and drops an intersection-probability factor in the final loss bound. Consequently, the central theoretical claim is unsupported.

The empirical mechanism conflicts with the headline claim that specialization emerges from implicit heterogeneity without task definitions. In the main quantity-skew setup, anchor clients are deliberately constructed from distinct label groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, supervised with expert-ID targets, and oversampled. This supplies explicit label-informed specialization structure. There is also no direct joint-versus-disjoint training ablation or convincing expert-diversity analysis to support the central causal claim.

The evaluation lacks independent-run counts, seed-level variation, confidence intervals, or statistical testing; the meaning of shaded regions is not defined. Several appendix tables select the best test accuracy during training, creating optimistic test-set checkpoint selection. Results are limited largely to synthetic label-skew partitions, and client routing aggregates the entire unseen client's test batch, making the claimed zero-shot setting transductive rather than ordinary per-example inference.

Comparisons do not isolate capacity or communication. DDOME stores 5–10 experts while FedMix uses two and other baselines use one model. In Table 1, both FedMix and DDOME transmit K=2 experts per client, so the claimed communication reduction is not demonstrated; DDOME additionally communicates a gate and requires an extra selection interaction. No measured bytes, latency, total computation, or parameter-matched comparison is provided.

Reproducibility and positioning are inadequate. There is no code link, and crucial details such as common-expert pretraining data/procedure, checkpoint construction, precise anchor selection, learning-rate decay, FedProx coefficient, baseline tuning budgets, aggregation details, and evaluation checkpoint policy are missing. Relevant personalized and clustered FL literature and stronger contemporary baselines are largely absent. Presentation defects—including DDOME being labeled FedJETs in plots, an AlexNet citation for Average Ensembles, ambiguous duplicate accuracy columns, and malformed proof notation—further obstruct verification.

The privacy claim is overstated: FL alone does not guarantee privacy, and communicated model updates and expert-selection identities can reveal client characteristics. The paper provides neither a privacy guarantee nor an analysis of this routing-specific leakage, despite presenting privacy preservation as a benefit.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant question: inducing useful expert specialization while limiting communication in heterogeneous decentralized learning. The motivation is compelling. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-d3yh36b4/call-9971996cb108467491fad3a498ecd777/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

DDOME combines a frozen common encoder, client-conditioned top-K routing, jointly updated experts/router, and anchor-based bootstrapping in an intuitive system. Label-free routing for unseen clients is potentially useful.

The empirical study spans CIFAR10/100, EMNIST, and Yahoo! Answers, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, incremental-client settings, and several ablations. Some reported gains over the implemented baselines are substantial.
The manuscript reports hardware and principal optimization settings and candidly acknowledges dependence on a strong common expert, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not technically supported. The final parameter uses a router optimized in Eq. (2), but the proof evaluates indicators induced by the random initial router and never analyzes the optimized router. The statement also places expectations over router initialization inside a probability claim over apparently the same randomness.

The proof contains additional consequential errors: an unmentioned and unproved covariance assumption is required; a maximum coordinate is incorrectly equated with an infinity norm; several inequality directions are reversed; a derived upper bound on an auxiliary vector is later used as a lower bound; overlap-probability factors are dropped from the loss bound; and projection/full-norm inequalities are mishandled. Even if repaired, the theorem concerns only one experts-first sequential procedure, not the claimed necessity of joint training generally, and it provides no positive result for joint training.

The core claim of semantic specialization is not directly evaluated. There are no expert-class affinities, utilization/load statistics, diversity measures, oracle-routing comparisons, or joint-versus-disjoint training ablation. Table 5 reports downstream classification errors without defining ground-truth routing correctness, so it does not demonstrate that the gate selects the appropriate expert.

Comparisons are not resource matched. DDOME maintains 5–10 full experts plus a common model, while FedAvg/FedProx use one model and the main FedMix comparison uses only two experts. Communication, parameter count, client storage, FLOPs, and inference cost are not quantified; in the main tables FedMix and DDOME both transmit two experts, so the asserted communication advantage is not established there.

Much of the apparent gain comes from baselines deteriorating far below their strong round-zero pretrained checkpoint. A keep-the-common-model or validation-based early-stopping baseline would dominate several reported methods and substantially reduce the headline improvement. The provenance, training data, and selection procedure for the unusually strong task-specific common checkpoints are not documented.

The anchor mechanism uses deliberately constructed label groups, one-to-one expert assignments, knowledge of distinct client distributions, and heavy oversampling—often half of every active cohort despite anchors comprising only 5–10% of clients. Performance largely fails without this mechanism. This weakens the claims that specialization arises from implicit heterogeneity without task definitions and raises deployment and fairness questions.

Statistical and reproducibility support is inadequate: no number of runs, uncertainty intervals, seeds, code, full preprocessing, MLP dimensions, checkpoint-selection protocol, or comparable hyperparameter-search budgets are supplied. Some results use the best observed accuracy, increasing selection bias, and several baseline collapses are insufficiently diagnosed.

The relationship to personalized, clustered, and newer federated MoE methods is too limited to justify the state-of-the-art claim. Evaluation is restricted to synthetic label-skew classification with 100 clients. Multiple figures still call the method “FedJETs,” the proof contains unresolved “(??)” references, and the claim of privacy-preserving FL is made without a threat model or privacy mechanism.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely problem: obtaining personalized expert specialization while limiting communication in heterogeneous decentralized learning.

The combination of a frozen common encoder, a learned client-conditioned router, sparse expert transfer, and anchor-based bootstrapping is a coherent system design with potentially useful practical applications.

The evaluation covers vision and text datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, and incremental-client scenarios. Ablations examine common-expert quality, anchor sampling, and per-sample routing behavior.

The main algorithm and system diagram communicate the intended workflow reasonably well, and the paper candidly acknowledges dependence on the common expert, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result appears false as stated. The main text uses x distributed with covariance I/sqrt(d), while the proof switches to I/d. With unit-norm orthogonal experts, the zero predictor has loss at most O(log(m)/sqrt(d)) under the former scaling and O(log(m)/d) under the latter. Because both sequential optimization stages can retain this feasible solution, the claimed Omega(1) final loss cannot hold asymptotically.

The proof has additional fatal gaps: its probability statement takes an expectation over the same random initialization over which it claims a high-probability event; Lemma 1 derives a high-probability conclusion from an ineffective tail inequality; the router event is incorrectly equated with a coordinate attaining the infinity norm; Appendix J defines the learned and ground-truth indicators identically; inequality directions needed to lower-bound the zeta vector are reversed; and the final loss bound drops routing probabilities and covariance scaling. Several dimensional assumptions also differ between the theorem and proof.

Even if repaired, Theorem 1 only analyzes one experts-first-then-router procedure in a stylized linear Gaussian model. It neither rules out other decoupled or alternating procedures nor proves that joint training converges successfully. It therefore does not establish the claimed general necessity of joint training or explain DDOME's deep federated setting.

The empirical specialization is not genuinely discovered without task information. Anchor clients are deliberately selected to have distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, and used with explicit one-hot expert targets for router training. The constructed anchors cover disjoint label groups, and the no-anchor ablation performs poorly. This substantially contradicts claims of specialization without explicit task boundaries or annotations.

Comparisons are not budget matched. DDOME stores 5–10 full experts, while FedMix uses two and other baselines use one or two models; active-client sampling, expert-update counts, initialization, and optimization also differ. No parameter, FLOP, wall-clock, client-compute, or transmitted-byte accounting supports the efficiency claim. In the main comparison, both FedMix and DDOME transmit two experts per normal client, so the asserted communication advantage is not directly demonstrated.

The headline accuracy gains rely heavily on poorly performing baselines. For example, methods initialized from a 93% CIFAR-10 common expert collapse as low as 43–71%, and the authors themselves attribute failures partly to incompatible learning rates. DDOME-specific optimization choices and incomplete baseline tuning make the claimed 4–24 point state-of-the-art improvement unconvincing; against the unchanged strong common expert, several gains are small.

Statistical and evaluation rigor is insufficient: there are no results across random seeds, uncertainty intervals, or significance tests; some appendix tables explicitly select the best test accuracy observed during training; and the numbers of test clients and checkpoint-selection protocol are unclear. Repeated use of the test set for model selection further weakens the evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite reporting some hardware and optimizer settings. There is no code link, and essential details—including common-expert training data and checkpoint construction, MLP dimensions, learning-rate decay, exact expert aggregation, sampling equivalence across baselines, and complete split generation—are missing. Terminology and presentation are also inconsistent, with DDOME labeled “FedJETs” in figures, duplicated “Acc.” columns, unresolved equation references, and numerous proof typos.

The related-work discussion and baseline set do not adequately cover modern personalized, clustered, and federated mixture approaches, so originality and state-of-the-art claims are not established. Experiments are limited to synthetic label-skew partitions, 100 simulated clients, and classification. Finally, calling the setup privacy-preserving is unsupported because no privacy mechanism or leakage analysis is provided. These issues, together with the invalid theorem, require new theory and substantial rerunning of the experiments rather than a rebuttal-scale correction.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: adaptive expert specialization and communication-efficient personalization for unseen decentralized clients. The combination of a frozen feature extractor, learned router, sparse expert transfer, and joint local updates is intuitive and clearly presented. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-b13znc0h/call-4ef53db08e96425d8d3cd36f1c78c148/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical study spans image and text classification, several label-skew constructions, incremental-client scenarios, and useful ablations on anchor frequency, common-expert quality, and expert count. DDOME reports substantial gains in some configurations.
The algorithm, system diagram, and discussion make the intended training and test-time workflows reasonably understandable.

The authors candidly identify important limitations, including dependence on a strong pretrained common expert, additional communication relative to single-model FL, limited scale, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not established. The theorem considers only one experts-first sequential procedure and never proves that joint training succeeds, so it cannot establish the necessity of joint training generally. More seriously, the proof appears invalid as written: it analyzes routing indicators from the initial random gate rather than the optimized gate in Equation (2), equates a maximum-coordinate event with an infinity-norm event, contains incorrect concentration/probability statements, and drops probability and covariance factors in the final loss lower bound.

The anchor mechanism conflicts with the claimed discovery of specialization without explicit task boundaries. Appendix A constructs anchors using label-distribution knowledge, deliberately covers label groups without replacement, permanently assigns each anchor to an expert, and oversamples these curated clients. This is effectively supervised routing information. The ablations show that DDOME struggles without it, making this assumption central rather than incidental.

The comparisons do not isolate the method's benefit fairly. DDOME uses 5–10 total experts and privileged anchor sampling, whereas the main FedMix comparison uses only two experts and the other baselines use one model. DDOME alone receives a different optimizer schedule in the text experiment. Baselines often catastrophically degrade a strong common checkpoint, yet competitive controls such as freezing, early stopping, lower-rate fine-tuning, matched anchor exposure, matched total capacity, and oracle or label-group routing are absent.

The headline 4–24% gains over state-of-the-art methods are therefore overstated. Against the unmodified common expert, several improvements are much smaller, including roughly 2.7 points on high-initialization CIFAR-10 and 0.5 points on high-initialization EMNIST. The baseline set also omits much of the personalized, clustered, and mixture-based federated-learning literature; a qualitative K-means plot is not an adequate comparison.

Statistical support is insufficient: results appear to come from single runs, with no variability across seeds or confidence intervals. Tables variously report unseen-client averages, best accuracy during training, or averages over the last evaluation rounds, making selection criteria and comparisons inconsistent.

Reproducibility is weak because no code is provided and critical details are missing, including the provenance and target-data exposure of common-expert checkpoints, full gate architecture, learning-rate decay, seed and hyperparameter-search protocols, precise client/test construction, and checkpoint selection. The use of sampling with replacement also leaves duplication and effective sample sizes unclear.

The communication and efficiency claims are not substantiated with bytes, FLOPs, latency, memory, or wall-clock comparisons. In the main comparison, both FedMix and DDOME transmit two full experts per client, while DDOME additionally transmits a gate and requires a two-stage selection exchange; thus reduced communication is not demonstrated under the reported configuration.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic label-skewed versions of standard classification datasets with 100 clients. This does not validate the broader claims about naturally emerging heterogeneity, real decentralized deployment, scalability, or semantic specialization. The description of FL as privacy-preserving is also unsupported without a threat model, secure aggregation, differential privacy, or leakage analysis.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely problem: communication-aware expert specialization for heterogeneous federated clients, including generalization to previously unseen clients.

DDOME has an understandable high-level design combining a frozen shared encoder, sparse expert routing, joint local updates, and anchor clients. Selecting K out of M experts could reduce per-client communication relative to transmitting the full expert pool.
The empirical study covers four datasets, vision and text modalities, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental-client scenarios, and several useful ablations.

The common-expert and anchor-ratio ablations expose important failure modes rather than hiding them, and the limitations section acknowledges dependence on pretrained representations and potential fairness risks.
The reported accuracy improvements are large enough to be practically interesting if confirmed under a more rigorous evaluation.
weaknesses: The central claim that specialization emerges from implicit heterogeneity without explicit task information is not supported. Anchor clients are deliberately selected to have distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, and used to train the gate with expert-ID targets. Performance deteriorates substantially without anchors, indicating that this explicit specialization supervision—not merely joint gate-expert training—is essential.

Theorem 1 is not technically valid as presented. The input covariance changes from I/sqrt(d) in the main text to I/d in the proof, while the claimed constant lower bound is incompatible with these scalings for allowed values such as m=1. The theorem also mixes a high-probability statement with an expectation over the same initialization and analyzes only one particular sequential procedure, which cannot establish the general necessity of joint training or show that joint training succeeds.

The proof contains additional material errors: the routed and ground-truth indicators are defined identically, a maximum-coordinate event is incorrectly replaced by a maximum-absolute-coordinate event, indices j and r are interchanged, inequality directions do not support the subsequent conclusion, intersection-probability factors are dropped in the final loss bound, and equation references remain unresolved. Thus the paper's main theoretical contribution is unsupported.

The experimental evidence lacks repeated trials, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Several baselines collapse far below their pretrained initialization, results sometimes use the best checkpoint rather than a fixed selection rule, and DDOME receives different optimizer treatment in the text experiment. These facts make the very large gains difficult to interpret and raise concerns about tuning fairness.

The comparisons do not control total model capacity: DDOME commonly maintains 5–10 experts while FedMix uses 2 and other baselines use one model. Many relevant personalized, clustered, and mixture-based federated-learning methods are omitted, so the state-of-the-art claim is not established.

The communication and efficiency claims are not substantiated with transmitted bytes, total communication, FLOPs, memory, latency, or accuracy-versus-resource curves. The common encoder, gate, extra experts, anchor oversampling, and up to 2,000 rounds must all be included in such accounting.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The provenance and training data of the common checkpoints, gate dimensions, learning-rate decay, aggregation weighting, exact client splits, sampling seeds, test-client construction, and checkpoint-selection procedures are insufficiently specified, and no code artifact is identified. Sampling data with replacement further requires explicit checks for duplication or leakage.

Presentation problems—including plots labeling the proposed method as “FedJETs,” two indistinguishable “Acc.” columns, ambiguous definitions of correct gate selection, duplicate references, and contradictory claims that the method is agnostic to common-expert quality—reduce clarity. Moreover, calling the setup privacy-preserving is too strong without a threat model, privacy mechanism, or analysis of information exposed by anchor selection and model updates.

strengths: The problem of adaptive expert specialization under federated heterogeneity is timely, and the frozen encoder, lightweight router, sparse expert dispatch, and anchor-client mechanism form an intuitively coherent system.
The evaluation covers four datasets across vision and text, unseen-client inference, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental learning, and useful ablations on anchors and common-expert quality.
The reported gains are substantial in several configurations, and the paper candidly discusses dependence on pretraining, communication overhead, scalability, and fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not established. Its high-probability statement contains an expectation over the same router initialization; the proof adds unstated assumptions and strengthens m≤√d to m≤√d/2; it analyzes routing induced by the initial V rather than the optimized router from Eq. (2); and it contains invalid inequality directions, including upper-bounding ||ζ|| by ||ζ̂|| and then using ζ̂ to obtain a lower bound. The final loss bound also drops an intersection-probability factor. Consequently, neither the theorem nor the broad claimed necessity of joint training follows. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-7u4yjat9/call-9bfcec3111ed48c68fd20624b64eb526/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The claimed unsupervised emergence of specialization conflicts with the anchor construction: anchors are deliberately selected for distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts corresponding to label groups, and heavily oversampled. This supplies explicit routing structure and assumes privileged knowledge whose availability is not operationalized.

Experimental reporting has no repeated trials, error bars, significance tests, or seeds. Several appendix tables report the best test accuracy during training, and common-expert checkpoints are characterized using accuracy thresholds, creating test-selection bias and preventing reliable assessment of the gains.

Comparisons are not adequately controlled. DDOME uses 5–10 experts while the main FedMix baseline uses only two; DDOME receives anchor supervision and, for text, a favorable optimizer schedule; several baselines collapse after starting from a strong checkpoint without convincing tuning or early stopping; and relevant personalized/clustered federated-learning baselines are largely absent.

The headline improvement is inflated by comparing against baselines that degrade far below the pretrained common expert. In some settings DDOME improves only modestly over that common expert or remains worse, despite using much greater model capacity and training cost.

Meaningful specialization is not actually demonstrated. Table 5 reports prediction errors rather than router correctness, and there are no expert-affinity, diversity, load-balancing, oracle-routing, or joint-versus-disjoint training measurements. Thus accuracy alone cannot support the proposed mechanism.

The communication and inference-efficiency claims lack byte-, FLOP-, latency-, or memory-level evaluation. In the main comparison, both DDOME and FedMix transmit two experts, while DDOME additionally communicates a router; inference also requires the common encoder plus a task expert.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the common-expert pretraining data and checkpoint procedure, router dimensions and activations, learning-rate decay, sparse aggregation details, validation protocol, client sample counts, and code are unspecified. Undefined labels such as “FedJETs,” an incorrect Average-Ensembles citation, and a mismatch between weighted top-K training and top-1 testing further reduce clarity and confidence.

Rating scale:
1 = Strong Reject
Fundamental deficiencies, a lack of substantive new contribution, or unresolved serious ethical issues rule out acceptance.

2 = Reject
Important shortcomings in technical support, evaluation, or reproducibility outweigh the paper's merits.

4 = Borderline accept
The work is technically solid and the reasons for acceptance slightly outweigh the remaining concerns. Please use sparingly.

5 = Accept
The paper offers a strong, well-supported contribution with meaningful impact and adequate reproducibility.

6 = Strong Accept
The work offers an exceptional and potentially field-changing contribution, with outstanding technical support and no unresolved material ethical concerns.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: adaptive expert specialization and reduced expert transmission in heterogeneous federated learning. The combination of a frozen common encoder, client-level routing, sparse expert dispatch, and anchor clients is intuitive and potentially useful.

The empirical study spans four datasets, vision and text architectures, two heterogeneity constructions, unseen-client evaluation, and incremental client-pool scenarios. Reported gains are often large.
Ablations examine common-expert quality, anchor-client frequency, and expert count, revealing useful practical dependencies and failure regimes.
The paper provides an algorithm, core hyperparameters, hardware/runtime information, and a candid limitations section discussing initialization, communication, scalability, and bias risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not technically supported and appears false as stated. It claims necessity from only one experts-first procedure and never proves joint training succeeds. Moreover, the stated Gaussian scaling makes the zero predictor's loss vanish for fixed m as d grows, contradicting an dimension-independent Omega(1) lower bound; m=1 is also an immediate counterexample.

The appendix has additional fatal proof gaps: the probability statement is combined incoherently with expectation over the same initialization; required assumptions are absent from the theorem; the initialized and ground-truth indicators are defined identically; the proof analyzes the initial router rather than the optimized router from Eq. 2; a maximum is incorrectly replaced by an infinity norm; several inequality directions and indices are wrong; probability factors are dropped; and unresolved '(??)' references remain.

The claimed necessity of joint router-expert training is not tested empirically with a controlled joint-versus-sequential ablation. The theory is also disconnected from DDOME's decentralized nonlinear, softmax-routed setting.

Success depends critically on privileged anchor construction: anchors are selected to have distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one expert identities, directly supervise the router with expert-ID targets, and occupy up to half of every round. DDOME fails without them. This substantially weakens the claim that specialization is discovered from implicit heterogeneity without explicit task structure and makes comparisons with uniformly sampled baselines questionable.

Baseline support is insufficient for a state-of-the-art claim. Main comparisons give DDOME 5-10 experts but FedMix only two, omit many personalized/clustered federated-learning methods, use a different optimizer and decay schedule for DDOME on text, and report several baseline collapses without reproducible tuning details or matched model, compute, and communication budgets.

Results lack numbers of runs, uncertainty estimates, significance tests, and a clear validation/model-selection protocol. Some appendix tables report the best test accuracy during training, creating test-set selection concerns. The provenance and training procedure of the unusually strong target-task common experts are also unclear.

The communication and efficiency claims are not quantified in bytes, FLOPs, memory, latency, or communication-to-target-accuracy. Sending two full experts plus a router can exceed FedAvg's per-round traffic, while the common encoder and server-side expert pool add unreported costs.

The evaluation does not directly establish expert specialization. Table 5 appears to measure final prediction correctness rather than routing correctness, and there are no expert-diversity, routing-oracle-gap, load-balancing, or specialization metrics. Test-time routing also uses the entire unlabeled target-client input collection, a transductive advantage not matched for baselines, so 'zero-shot' requires qualification.

Reproducibility and clarity are below acceptance level: no code link is provided; partitioning 'with replacement,' client sizes, anchor selection, aggregation weighting, learning-rate decay, and several testing details are underspecified. Tables contain unlabeled duplicate accuracy columns, figures retain the obsolete name 'FedJETs,' and the algorithm and prose contain numerous notation and editing errors.

The privacy discussion is overly positive: standard federated updates are not automatically privacy-preserving, and repeated participation plus label-distribution-based anchor selection introduces privacy and participation-fairness concerns without threat-model or leakage analysis.
