strengths: The manuscript addresses a timely problem: adaptive expert specialization and economical routing under decentralized, heterogeneous data. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-jri0jjpy/call-fdc9fdb284da44829422fd68f5e6d599/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

DDOME combines a frozen common encoder, client-conditioned top-K routing, jointly updated experts/router, and an anchor-based warm start into an intuitive system. The overview figure and algorithm communicate the intended workflow reasonably well.

The reported point estimates are promising in several settings, especially CIFAR-10/100 and Yahoo! Answers, and the evaluation spans vision and text, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, unseen clients, and incremental client populations.
The ablations concerning common-expert quality, anchor-client ratio, and expert-pool size expose important practical dependencies rather than presenting the method as universally reliable.

Hardware, training time, and several optimization hyperparameters are reported, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on pretrained encoders, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness harms.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established by the supplied proof. The proof analyzes routing regions induced by the initialized router but never analyzes the optimized router from Eq. (2); it also defines I_j and I_j* identically, contains an invalid concentration argument, reverses a key inequality on page 25, and drops the routing-intersection probability in the final loss lower bound. Probability and expectation are also taken over the same initialization, and the Gaussian scaling and m-versus-d conditions differ between the statement and proof.

Even a repaired theorem would only show failure of one experts-first procedure with a random frozen router in a stylized population linear-Gaussian model. It neither proves that joint training succeeds nor analyzes DDOME, anchors, finite client data, federated aggregation, soft routing, or classification. Thus the claimed necessity of joint training is substantially overstated.

The claim of discovering specialization without explicit task boundaries conflicts with the anchor mechanism. Anchors are deliberately selected to have distinct label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, and train the router with expert-ID labels. In the main CIFAR-10 setting, all five anchors participate every round and collectively cover label groups. Performance without this curated, heavily oversampled supervision deteriorates sharply.

The empirical comparison is not adequately controlled. DDOME maintains 5–10 experts while important baselines use one or two; the text experiments give DDOME a different optimizer and learning-rate schedule; and baselines do not appear to receive the same stratified anchor sampling. Relevant personalized, clustered, and newer federated-MoE methods are largely absent, undermining the state-of-the-art claim.

Results are point estimates without independent runs, uncertainty, or significance tests. Several tables report the best test accuracy during training or among final test evaluations without a validation-based selection protocol. Many baselines collapse far below their starting common expert, so a practical retain-or-early-stop baseline would materially narrow the claimed gains.

The common expert is the method's critical component, yet its pretraining data, procedure, checkpoint-selection protocol, and disjointness from evaluation data are insufficiently specified. Exact partitions, random seeds, decay schedule, aggregation weighting for sparsely updated experts, and tuning budgets are also missing, and no code artifact is provided.

The communication and inference-efficiency claims lack measurements of transmitted bytes, FLOPs, latency, storage, or accuracy at matched budgets. In the main comparison, FedMix and DDOME both send two experts per selected client, while DDOME additionally maintains a larger pool and communicates a router; test-time execution also requires the common encoder, router, and selected expert.

Meaningful specialization is not directly demonstrated. Per-expert global accuracy does not show distinct semantic functions, and Table 5 never defines what constitutes a correct routing decision when no ground-truth expert exists. Assignment matrices, expert diversity, load balance, label/domain affinity, and oracle-routing comparisons are needed to distinguish specialization from increased capacity and anchor supervision.

Presentation problems impede verification: two main result columns share the label “Acc.”, several figures call DDOME “FedJETs,” the proof contains unresolved “(??)” references and duplicated assumptions, and the relationship to prior federated personalization/MoE work is underdeveloped. These issues, together with the unsupported theorem and confounded evaluation, are too substantial for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The problem of adaptive expert specialization for decentralized, non-IID data is timely and potentially useful. The proposed combination of a frozen encoder, learned router, sparse top-K expert transmission, and label-free routing for unseen clients is a coherent systems idea.

The evaluation covers four vision and text datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, and several useful ablations involving anchor frequency, common-expert quality, expert count, and changing client pools.
The manuscript acknowledges important limitations, including dependence on a strong pretrained model, additional communication, limited scale, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not valid as presented. The statement takes probability and expectation over the same initialization, permits the immediate counterexample m=1, and uses an input scaling under which even the trivial predictor has vanishing loss for fixed m, contradicting the claimed dimension-independent lower bound. The appendix defines the learned and ground-truth routing indicators identically, invokes an unstated assumption, changes the Gaussian scaling and the condition on m, contains incorrect inequality directions and dimensionally invalid expressions, and ultimately evaluates the initialized router rather than the optimized router from Equation 2. Thus, it does not establish the claimed necessity of joint training.

The empirical setup contradicts the claimed discovery of specialization from implicit heterogeneity. Anchor clients are deliberately selected for distinct—and, in the quantity-based experiments, non-overlapping—label groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, oversampled in 30–50% of each round, and used to train the router with explicit one-hot expert targets. Performance largely fails without this privileged structure.

Comparisons are substantially confounded. DDOME has 5–10 full expert models plus a router and common model, versus mostly single-model baselines; it also receives a different optimizer schedule on Yahoo. Several baselines collapse from strong pretrained checkpoints, and the authors explicitly attribute this partly to inconsistent learning rates. There are no capacity-, computation-, or tuning-matched comparisons, and the near-random SCAFFOLD and domain-generalization results raise implementation-validity concerns.

The reported gains are statistically unsupported: no number of runs, seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are given. Some tables select the best test accuracy during training or an accuracy envelope, apparently using the test set for checkpoint selection. Weak common checkpoints for which the method fails are selectively excluded from headline tables.

The necessary common experts already obtain 61–93% task accuracy, yet their training data and checkpoint construction are not specified. On several settings, much of the headline gain over prior methods comes from comparing against baselines that degraded far below this unchanged common expert rather than against a competitive retained or personalized checkpoint.

The communication-efficiency claim is not evaluated in bytes, total communication, computation, latency, memory, or inference cost. Sending K=2 full experts plus a router can exceed FedAvg communication; the claim is demonstrated only relative to FedMix sending every expert, while preprocessing and storing embeddings for every local example are ignored.

Reproducibility is inadequate: there is no code link, and essential details such as MLP dimensions, common-expert provenance, aggregation weighting, complete hyperparameter searches, run counts, checkpoint selection, and precise test-client construction are absent. The related-work discussion also omits important personalized and clustered federated-learning alternatives, weakening the originality case.

The manuscript appears unfinished: plots retain the former name “FedJETs,” tables have two identically labeled accuracy columns, the proof contains unresolved “(??)” references, citations are duplicated or mismatched, and several algorithmic quantities are undefined. The claim that the method provides privacy-preserving FL is also unsupported because neither differential privacy nor secure aggregation is used.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: efficient, zero-label personalization of mixture-of-experts models for heterogeneous decentralized clients.
DDOME is conceptually coherent, combining a fixed pretrained encoder, sparse per-client routing, joint local optimization, and anchor-assisted specialization.
The evaluation spans four image and text datasets, multiple heterogeneity constructions, unseen clients, incremental settings, and several useful ablations. Reported gains are often large.
The paper openly reports dependence on common-expert quality, computational cost, scalability limits, and possible fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is unsupported. Theorem 1 only concerns one expert-first sequential procedure and never proves that joint training succeeds or that every decoupled alternative fails. Its proof also appears invalid: it conflates initialized and optimized routing, relies on an unstated/unproved covariance assumption, contains incoherent probability quantifiers and reversed inequalities, uses an upper bound on an auxiliary quantity as a lower bound, and drops routing-intersection probabilities when lower-bounding the final loss. Unresolved equation references remain in the proof.

The claimed emergence of specialization without explicit task boundaries is misleading. Anchor clients are deliberately constructed or selected for distinct label distributions, fixed one-to-one to experts, and used to supervise the router with expert-ID targets. Performance deteriorates substantially without this mechanism.

Comparisons are not resource- or optimization-matched. DDOME has 5–10 experts while major baselines have one model and FedMix usually has two; DDOME receives method-specific learning-rate decay for text; and no controlled parameter, FLOP, or communication-to-accuracy comparison is provided. Downloading two experts also exceeds FedAvg's one-model communication.

Most baselines fall far below the untouched pretrained common expert, making the large improvement claims difficult to interpret. Baseline tuning is insufficiently documented, stronger personalized/clustered federated-learning and recent federated-MoE baselines are missing, and the related-work coverage is dated.

There are no multi-seed results, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Some tables select the best test accuracy observed during training without a validation protocol, and sampling data with replacement can duplicate examples across clients. Test-time routing also aggregates the client's entire unlabeled test set, making the advertised zero-shot setting transductive.

The paper does not directly establish semantic expert specialization: it lacks utilization, diversity, expert-label alignment, or oracle-routing analyses and lacks an empirical joint-versus-sequential training ablation. Its reported per-sample routing table measures final classification errors rather than whether the correct expert was selected.

Reproducibility and clarity are inadequate: no code artifact is identified, aggregation and checkpoint-selection details remain ambiguous, figures call the proposed method “FedJETs,” the proof contains unresolved “??” references and inconsistent notation, and the privacy-preserving characterization is unsupported by a threat model or privacy mechanism.

Several reported gains are potentially meaningful, particularly under the weaker common-expert and Dirichlet settings. The method also routes unseen clients without requiring their labels or full-model fine-tuning.

The system diagram and high-level training procedure are understandable, and the paper honestly acknowledges dependence on a strong common expert, communication overhead, limited scale, tuning complexity, and possible fairness harms. No material research-ethics issue arises from the public benchmark experiments themselves.
weaknesses: The central theorem is false as written. For m=1, the sole expert trained in step (1) exactly recovers the sole ground-truth linear expert, yielding zero parameter error and zero loss, directly contradicting both Ω(1) conclusions. More generally, under the stated covariance x∼N(0,I/√d), the zero-expert loss vanishes for fixed m, and the two optimization stages cannot have larger optimum loss than this feasible solution. The appendix also drops the 1/d covariance factor and routing-event probability in its final lower bound, invokes an unproved assumption absent from the theorem statement, uses a dimensionally invalid decomposition of w*, and contains inconsistent dimensional and concentration claims.

Even a corrected failure result for this particular experts-first-then-router procedure would not prove that joint training is necessary in general. It neither excludes other decoupled or alternating procedures nor establishes that joint optimization succeeds. There is also no controlled joint-versus-disjoint empirical ablation, so the paper's main theoretical conclusion is substantially overstated and disconnected from DDOME.

The claimed discovery of specialization without explicit task boundaries is undermined by the anchor construction. In the principal quantity-skew experiments, anchors are deliberately created as disjoint label groups covering the classes, assigned one-to-one to experts, and heavily oversampled. Performance struggles without this mechanism. Thus much of the specialization is seeded with explicit label-based structure rather than discovered solely from implicit heterogeneity. All client distributions are synthetic label-skew partitions rather than natural federated populations.

The headline comparisons are confounded. FedMix has only two total experts while DDOME has pools of five or ten; nevertheless, both transmit two experts per client in the main experiments, so the claimed communication reduction is not demonstrated by that comparison. Single-model baselines transmit less. No byte-level, total-to-accuracy, memory, or inference-cost results are reported. In the matched M=K CIFAR10 experiment, DDOME remains below the unmodified common expert.

Several baselines collapse far below their pretrained starting checkpoint, including FedAvg and SCAFFOLD, raising substantial implementation or tuning concerns. The advertised 24-point gain on CIFAR10 compares DDOME at 95.7% against degraded trained baselines while the no-training common expert already achieves 93%. Strong personalized and clustered-FL methods are omitted, and Appendix I replaces a quantitative clustering comparison with a single qualitative K-means plot.

The statistical and diagnostic evidence is insufficient: there are no independent-run variances, confidence intervals, or reported seeds. Some tables select the best test accuracy during training and figures use test-accuracy envelopes without a stated validation protocol. Table 5 reports final classification correctness, not whether the gate selected the best expert, and the paper lacks routing accuracy, load, diversity, specialization, random-router, or oracle-router analyses.

Reproducibility is poor. There is no code or artifact, and the source and training procedure for the task-specific common experts—on which results critically depend—are not specified. Exact client/test splits, checkpoint identifiers, MLP dimensions, learning-rate decay, FedProx coefficient, baseline search spaces, aggregation details, and several sample counts are missing or ambiguous. The related-work treatment is also incomplete and contains duplicated or mismatched citations and inconsistent method naming in figures. Collectively, the invalid theory and inadequately controlled evaluation outweigh the promising system idea.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-pifddbxr/call-f17ab420548248048a2c705ed3f6620a/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a timely problem: communication-efficient, zero-shot personalization using decentralized mixtures of experts.

DDOME combines a frozen common encoder, sparse expert transfer, joint router-expert updates, and anchor clients into an intuitively coherent system. Selecting only K of M experts could reduce communication relative to full-MoE approaches such as FedMix.

The empirical scope includes vision and text datasets, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, unseen clients, incremental client pools, and ablations of common-expert quality and anchor-client frequency. The reported gains in the chosen settings are substantial.

The paper is candid about dependence on a strong pretrained encoder, anchor-client tuning, limited scale, and possible fairness risks. Its high-level motivation and system diagram are generally understandable.
weaknesses: The central theorem is false as stated. For m=1, the only router assigns every input to the only expert, so population least squares in Eq. (1) exactly recovers w* and has zero loss, directly contradicting both claimed Omega(1) conclusions. The assertion that labels have constant magnitude is also inconsistent with x distributed as N(0, I/sqrt(d)) and unit-norm experts.

The proof contains further material gaps: it relies on an assumption absent from the theorem statement; strengthens m <= sqrt(d) to m <= sqrt(d)/2; incorrectly replaces a coordinate maximum with an infinity norm; contains unjustified or reversed inequalities in the zeta argument; inconsistently indexes the comparator expert; and never rigorously analyzes the router obtained by the second-stage optimization. Broken equation references such as '(??)' further impede verification.

Even if repaired, a failure result for one particular experts-first sequential procedure would not establish that joint training is generally necessary. The analysis neither proves that joint training succeeds nor models DDOME's common encoder, anchor clients, top-K selection, aggregation, or federated optimization, so the theoretical and algorithmic contributions are weakly connected.

The key 'implicit heterogeneity without explicit task definitions' claim is undermined by the evaluation design. Anchor clients are deliberately constructed using labels to cover distinct class groups, assigned one-to-one to experts, and heavily oversampled—often providing half of every round's updates. This is strong task information, biases the nominal client-average objective, and lacks a practical label-free anchor-selection procedure.

The empirical comparison is not reliable enough for the claims. Several baselines collapse dramatically below the frozen common expert—for example, methods initialized at 93.05% attain 28.24–41.83%, while DDOME itself reaches only 87.86%—yet the paper still presents this as favorable. Hyperparameter budgets, early stopping, and client-compute controls are not standardized, while results variously use averages, the best point during training, or the best of the last ten evaluations, apparently based on test curves without a validation protocol.

There are no repeated-run statistics, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Reproduction-critical details are missing, including how the highly task-accurate common checkpoints were trained and what data they used, exact router architecture, anchor identification, expert-wise aggregation weights, learning-rate decay, baseline tuning, checkpoint selection, preprocessing, and random seeds; no code or artifact is identified.

Expert specialization—the paper's central empirical claim—is not directly measured. Table 5 reports prediction correctness rather than whether routing selected an appropriate expert, and the paper lacks per-label/domain expert performance, routing-oracle comparisons, utilization/load balance, diversity measures, or collapse diagnostics.

Communication efficiency is asserted from K < M rather than evaluated in bytes, total communication, latency, memory, or client computation. The analysis omits common-model distribution, local embedding and storage, router transmission, expert-index negotiation, and the fact that DDOME communicates multiple models compared with single-model FL baselines.

Related work and baselines are too limited to substantiate state-of-the-art claims, especially for personalized/clustered federated learning and more recent federated MoE methods. Presentation errors—including duplicate 'Acc.' columns, plots labeled 'FedJETs' instead of DDOME, repeated 'Ensemble' artifacts, and undefined aggregation operations—add ambiguity. Privacy-preserving deployment is also claimed without a privacy mechanism or analysis of leakage through routing and updates.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely problem: adaptive expert specialization and sparse model dispatch for heterogeneous decentralized clients. The frozen encoder, lightweight router, expert pool, and test-time routing form a concrete system.

The empirical study spans vision and text classification, four datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, incremental-client scenarios, and several ablations. Some reported gains are large within the paper's protocol.

The common-expert-quality and anchor-ratio ablations expose important operating conditions, including the method's strong dependence on sufficiently informative representations and frequent anchor participation.

The presentation includes an algorithm, principal optimization settings, hardware and runtime information, and a candid limitations section. The public datasets raise no immediate research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not established. Among other problems, the proof defines the learned and ground-truth routing indicators identically, substitutes an infinity-norm event for a maximum-coordinate event, applies a projection bound without an assumed relationship between the ground-truth router and expert subspaces, reverses a key inequality involving the auxiliary zeta vectors, and drops routing-region probabilities in the final loss bound. Its high-probability statement also takes an expectation over the same initialization, and the proof does not correctly analyze the reoptimized router.

Even if repaired, Theorem 1 only concerns one expert-first-then-router population procedure in a linear Gaussian hard-routing model. It neither proves that joint optimization succeeds nor establishes general necessity, and it is poorly connected to DDOME's softmax, top-K, anchor-based federated algorithm. There is no corresponding joint-versus-disjoint empirical ablation.

The claimed discovery of specialization without explicit task boundaries is undermined by the anchor mechanism. Anchors are deliberately constructed or selected for distinct label distributions, manually assigned one-to-one to experts, and provide one-hot expert supervision to the router. They comprise 30–50% of participants per round, and the no-anchor ablation largely fails. Baselines are not given comparable distribution knowledge or sampling.

The comparisons are not capacity-, computation-, or optimization-matched: DDOME maintains 5–10 experts while FedMix commonly has two and standard FL baselines have one; DDOME alone receives a different optimizer schedule for text. Several baselines catastrophically degrade from 73–93% pretrained checkpoints, and the authors explicitly attribute this partly to learning-rate mismatch, making the large gains unconvincing evidence of algorithmic superiority.

Important personalized, clustered, and mixture-based FL comparisons are absent, such as IFCA/FedEM-style methods and modern personalized FL approaches. A qualitative K-means plot is not an adequate substitute. The related-work treatment is very limited, and the Average Ensembles citation incorrectly points to the AlexNet paper.

The provenance, training data, and cost of the task-specific common experts—reaching up to 93% accuracy—are unspecified. If these models were centrally trained on the same task data, that materially changes the federated-learning premise. Moreover, the reported 'zero-shot' protocol is transductive: DDOME uses each test client's entire unlabeled collection for routing, without giving baselines an analogous adaptation mechanism.

There are no repeated-run means, standard deviations, defined uncertainty bands, or significance tests. Client construction, sample counts, replacement, checkpoint selection, aggregation weighting, MLP dimensions, decay schedule, and baseline searches remain insufficiently specified. No code or artifact is supplied.

The communication-efficiency claim is unsupported by byte, FLOP, memory, or wall-clock comparisons. In the main experiments FedMix sends two experts and DDOME also sends two, while DDOME additionally communicates a router and requires a common encoder; total system capacity and training cost are not accounted for.

The experiments do not directly establish semantic specialization: Table 5 reports prediction correctness rather than a defined routing target, and there are no expert-diversity, utilization, load-balance, oracle-routing, or random-routing analyses. Figures also inconsistently label DDOME as 'FedJETs,' and evaluation metrics alternate ambiguously between personalized, global, average, and best-checkpoint accuracy.

Evaluation is limited to artificial label-skew partitions of at most 100 clients. Claims of privacy preservation lack a threat model or privacy guarantee, while selecting anchors by client distributions may itself require sensitive distributional knowledge. Overall, the invalid theory and heavily confounded evaluation outweigh the method's promising system idea.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant problem: communication-aware, label-free personalization for unseen federated clients using sparse expert routing. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6vrtv0kr/call-e6979e2cd1aa4dbba3713303e5713d19/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The combination of a frozen common encoder, client-conditioned top-K routing, jointly updated experts, and anchor clients is intuitive and described at a reasonably understandable high level.
The evaluation covers four image/text datasets, two synthetic heterogeneity schemes, incremental-client scenarios, and ablations concerning anchors, initialization, and expert count.

The authors candidly acknowledge dependence on a sufficiently accurate common expert, additional communication, limited scalability, and possible fairness risks. The reported improvements would be meaningful if validated under a rigorous protocol.
weaknesses: The central theorem is false as stated. Taking m=1, which satisfies m≤√d, makes the router select the sole expert for every sample; population least squares recovers w* exactly and achieves zero loss, directly contradicting both Ω(1) conclusions. The appendix also changes the input covariance from I/√d to I/d, omits corresponding covariance factors, reverses inequalities when passing from ζ to its upper bound, and contains incorrect concentration/probability reasoning. Thus the claimed rigorous justification does not hold.

Even if repaired, the theorem only concerns one particular experts-first-then-router procedure with random linear top-1 routing on Gaussian data. It neither proves that joint training is generally necessary nor analyzes DDOME's soft routing, anchor mechanism, federated aggregation, or convergence.

The experimental evidence lacks repeated trials, error bars, statistical tests, and a clear validation protocol. Several appendices explicitly report the best test accuracy during training or averages over test evaluations, suggesting test-driven checkpoint or hyperparameter selection. Common-expert checkpoints are also selected post hoc around the threshold where DDOME begins improving.

Baseline credibility and fairness are major concerns. Several methods catastrophically collapse from strong pretrained checkpoints, tuning is described only vaguely, DDOME receives a different optimizer and decay schedule on text, and the main FedMix comparison uses fewer total experts than DDOME. There are no controlled comparisons at matched model capacity, computation, communication, and tuning budget across the main datasets.

The work omits central personalized, clustered, and mixture-based federated-learning comparators; a K-means visualization is not an adequate substitute. It also lacks competitive approaches that can exploit unlabeled client data at test time, although DDOME uses the entire test client's local batch to select experts. Consequently, the state-of-the-art claim and the novelty relative to prior federated MoE work are not established.

The anchor-client mechanism conflicts with the claim of discovering specialization from implicit heterogeneity without task annotations. Experiments deliberately construct anchors with distinct or non-overlapping label distributions and map them one-to-one to experts, requiring privileged knowledge of client label composition. No practical private anchor-discovery method, robustness analysis for poor anchors, or assessment of the disproportionate participation burden is provided.

Efficiency claims are not quantitatively supported: there are no transmitted-byte, FLOP, latency, memory, or energy measurements accounting for the gate, initial common encoder, K full experts, M-model server storage, and frequent anchor participation. DDOME is only shown to transmit fewer experts than FedMix, while remaining substantially heavier than single-model methods.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code is identified, and important details such as seeds, common-expert training and checkpoint selection, learning-rate decay, baseline search spaces, exact client/test construction, aggregation weighting, and checkpoint selection are missing. Presentation inconsistencies—including figures labeling DDOME as “FedJETs,” ambiguous duplicate “Acc.” columns, and unclear per-sample routing metrics—further obstruct verification.

The privacy language is overstated: ordinary federated averaging is not inherently privacy-preserving, and no threat model, secure aggregation, differential privacy, or gradient-leakage analysis is supplied. The paper mentions fairness risks but does not evaluate them.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely problem: obtaining useful expert specialization and sparse communication in heterogeneous decentralized learning. The combination of client-level routing, a frozen representation model, and sparse expert dispatch is potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/neurips2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bp8cv6dv/call-949f9e6d889f4d37aebc81b38a2e5246/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

DDOME is intuitively structured, and its ability to route unseen clients without test-label fine-tuning is attractive. The anchor-client warm start is a practical response to early routing instability.

The empirical section covers image and text classification, quantity- and Dirichlet-based heterogeneity, several FL baselines, incremental-client scenarios, and ablations of the common expert and anchor ratio. The reported gains are large enough to motivate further study.
The paper candidly identifies dependence on the pretrained encoder, anchor tuning, communication overhead, limited scale, and possible fairness risks. No acute unresolved ethical issue is apparent.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not established and is false in at least one stated case: for m=1, expert-first training exactly recovers the sole ground-truth linear expert, contradicting the claimed constant error. More generally, Eq. (2) optimizes a new router, but the appendix continues using indicators from the initialized router and therefore bounds the pre-rerouting loss, not L(hat theta). A lower bound before router optimization cannot lower-bound the optimized loss.

The proof has additional material defects: an unstated and unproved Assumption 2, inconsistent Gaussian scaling between the theorem and appendix, m≤sqrt(d) versus a step requiring m≤sqrt(d)/2, inconsistent probability exponents, unresolved equation references, index confusion, and a reversed inequality near the definition of hat-zeta. Moreover, failure of one experts-first schedule would not by itself prove that joint training is necessary or that joint training succeeds.

The central causal claim is not tested empirically: there is no controlled joint-versus-disjoint router/expert training ablation. Nor is semantic specialization measured directly through routing entropy, expert usage, diversity, or oracle assignments; aggregate accuracy alone does not establish meaningful specialization.

The headline “implicit heterogeneity without task boundaries” claim conflicts with the main anchor construction. Quantity-based experiments deliberately choose anchors with disjoint label groups, assign each one to a unique expert, train the gate with one-hot expert targets, and heavily oversample anchors. This introduces explicit label-partition supervision and assumes knowledge and control that may be unavailable in realistic federated deployments.

The empirical comparisons are insufficiently controlled. DDOME uses 5–10 full experts while most baselines use one and FedMix uses two; there is no parameter-, compute-, or tuning-budget-matched control. Results lack repeated seeds, uncertainty, or significance tests, and key baselines often catastrophically degrade from the same strong pretrained initialization. DDOME also receives a different optimizer/schedule for text, while baseline tuning details and checkpoint-selection rules are incomplete.

The claimed communication benefit is not quantified in bytes, latency, or total computation. In the main comparisons, both DDOME and FedMix transmit two experts per normal client, while DDOME additionally communicates a gate, requires a common encoder and an extra selection interaction, and stores a substantially larger server-side pool.

Generality and reproducibility remain limited: evaluation uses synthetic label partitions of standard centralized datasets and apparently only 5–10 unseen clients in key analyses, rather than natural federated/domain shifts. There is no code link, and important details such as exact pretrained checkpoints, gate width, per-client sample counts, random seeds, partial-expert aggregation, and full baseline configurations are missing. Sampling “with replacement” also leaves cross-client duplication unclear. Undefined “FedJETs” plot labels and an incorrect citation for Average Ensembles further reduce clarity. These combined theoretical and empirical shortcomings require major revision and outweigh the promising idea.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: communication-efficient, zero-label personalization with sparse mixtures of experts in decentralized learning.
DDOME is conceptually coherent and reasonably well described through its frozen common encoder, client-level top-K routing, expert pool, anchor mechanism, losses, and pseudocode.

The empirical study spans vision and text classification, four datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, and useful ablations involving common-expert quality, anchor frequency, expert initialization, and changing client pools.

The reported accuracy gains are substantial in several synthetic federated settings, and selecting K experts from a larger pool could reduce client communication relative to methods that transmit every expert.

The authors candidly acknowledge dependence on the common expert, communication overhead, limited scale, tuning complexity, and possible fairness risks. Architectures, basic optimizer settings, hardware, and runtimes are also reported.
weaknesses: The central theorem is not technically reliable as written. The data covariance is 1/sqrt(d) in the theorem but 1/d in the proof; the appendix defines the learned and ground-truth routing indicators identically; Assumption 2 is unstated in the theorem and is not valid uniformly over arbitrary positive-definite covariances; several probability and inequality directions are inconsistent; and routing-probability factors appear to be dropped in the final loss bound. Moreover, failure of one experts-then-router procedure does not establish that joint training is necessary or that joint optimization succeeds.

The claim of discovering specialization without explicit task boundaries conflicts with the anchor construction. Anchors are deliberately selected to have distinct, sometimes non-overlapping label sets, assigned one-to-one expert targets, trained with one-hot routing labels, and heavily oversampled. This supplies strong prior task structure and could itself explain the specialization.

There is no empirical joint-versus-disjoint training ablation, despite this being the headline claim. The available ablation instead shows that DDOME performs poorly without the supervised anchor mechanism.

The main comparisons are confounded. DDOME uses 5 or 10 total experts while FedMix generally uses 2; optimizer scheduling differs in the Yahoo experiments; baseline tuning is unspecified; and continued training makes several baselines catastrophically worse than their already-strong initialization. A checkpoint-selection strategy should at least preserve the common expert's starting accuracy.

Results are reported without repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite visibly unstable learning curves. It is also unclear whether tables use final, average, peak, or best-of-last-round performance, making the large improvement claims difficult to verify.

Communication and efficiency claims are not supported by transmitted-byte, latency, compute, memory, or energy measurements. The costs of the common encoder, router, and larger server-side expert pool are not included in a controlled accuracy-versus-cost comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code is provided, and important details such as common-expert training and checkpoint selection, MLP dimensions, decay schedule, FedProx coefficient and tuning ranges, aggregation when experts receive unequal numbers of updates, exact test-client construction, and model-selection protocol are missing.

The evaluation is limited to constructed label-skew simulations with 100 clients and a task-trained common expert whose quality must exceed an observed threshold. More realistic federated shifts, larger-scale deployments, and stronger recent personalized-FL or federated-MoE baselines are needed before claiming state of the art.

Presentation errors further reduce confidence: plots label the proposed method as "FedJETs," the Average Ensembles citation points to AlexNet rather than an ensemble method, and the purported per-sample routing evaluation reports classification errors without a ground-truth routing metric. The claim of privacy-preserving FL also lacks a threat model or formal privacy mechanism.

strengths: Addresses a timely problem: communication-efficient expert specialization and zero-shot personalization under federated data heterogeneity.
DDOME is a concrete, understandable design combining a frozen encoder, sparse expert routing, joint gate-expert updates, and anchor-based stabilization.

The experiments span four image/text datasets, two heterogeneity constructions, unseen clients, incremental learning, and several ablations. Some reported gains are substantial under the selected settings.
The manuscript reports hardware and training time, discusses practical dependencies and scalability limits, and acknowledges potential fairness risks.
weaknesses: The central theorem is invalid as written. Section 3 samples x from a Gaussian with covariance I/sqrt(d), while Appendix J uses I/d. With unit-norm experts, the zero predictor then has vanishing MSE, contradicting the claimed constant lower bound. The proof also drops covariance and routing-event factors, changes the condition from m <= sqrt(d) to m <= sqrt(d)/2, invokes an unstated/unproved assumption, and has inconsistent probability-versus-expectation quantifiers.

The proof continues to use the initialized routing regions and never analyzes the optimized second-stage router in Equation (2). More fundamentally, failure of one expert-first sequential procedure neither proves that joint training is necessary nor establishes that DDOME's joint optimization succeeds or converges.

The claimed emergence of specialization without explicit task definitions is undermined by the anchor mechanism. Anchors are chosen to have distinct, often non-overlapping label distributions, assigned one-to-one to experts, heavily oversampled, and used to supervise the gate with expert IDs. The no-anchor ablation shows that performance largely fails without this privileged structure.

Expert specialization is not directly demonstrated. The paper lacks class/domain-wise expert behavior, routing entropy, load balance, diversity, or oracle-routing analyses. The purported per-sample gating evaluation is essentially classification error, not accuracy against a well-defined correct expert, so gains could instead arise from additional capacity and anchor supervision.

Comparisons are not adequately controlled. DDOME uses 5-10 experts plus a gate and encoder, while several baselines use one model or two experts; computation, parameter count, client exposure, and communication bytes are not matched. DDOME alone also receives a different optimizer and learning-rate schedule in the text experiments.

Statistical and reproducibility support is insufficient: there are no repeated-run uncertainties, confidence intervals, or seeds; some tables report the best test accuracy observed during training without a validation protocol; exact common-expert provenance, gate architecture, decay schedule, aggregation details, and baseline tuning are incomplete; and no code is provided. The unexplained use of the name “FedJETs” for DDOME in figures further reduces confidence.

The method depends strongly on carefully selected target-task common-expert checkpoints and fails below an empirical threshold. In several high-quality-checkpoint settings it improves only marginally, and in the domain-generalization table the unchanged common expert outperforms DDOME. How such checkpoints are trained without compromising the decentralized premise is unclear.

Coverage of closely related personalized, clustered, and mixture-based federated learning is too limited to establish originality or state-of-the-art status. Evaluation is also confined to synthetic label partitions, 100 clients, and at most 10 experts, while the claimed communication advantage is never measured end to end.
